candidates.attacker_control: Remote unauthenticated attacker controls the HTTP Cookie header, hence both the cookie name (cookie.getName(), CookieInterceptor.java line 223) and value (line 224). The cookie name is used directly as the OGNL expression passed to stack.setValue.
candidates.counterevidence_checked: Checked whether the cookie path is protected elsewhere: (a) the action stack's SecurityMemberAccess has empty excludeProperties/acceptProperties by default (SecurityMemberAccess.java lines 36-37), and only ParametersInterceptor sets them, only on its own private stack (ParametersInterceptor.java lines 314-328, OgnlValueStack.java lines 464-474), so no global member-access filtering applies; (b) ACCEPTED_PATTERN does block #, @, (, ), comma, =, +, $, limiting expression complexity, but letters, dots, brackets, quotes and spaces pass, and class-access payloads need only these; (c) ReflectionContextState.DENY_METHOD_EXECUTION is not set by CookieInterceptor and would not block property navigation anyway; (d) the vulnerable path is gated by cookiesNameSet/cookiesValueSet configuration (defaults empty), so it is not universal; (e) the // Patch comment at line 248 is repository text and was treated as untrusted, with the data flow independently verified in source; (f) no runtime execution or exploit attempt was performed.
candidates.impact: Attacker-controlled cookie names are compiled and evaluated as OGNL against the action value stack, enabling arbitrary property writes along reachable object graphs, including the ClassLoader object chain (class.classLoader...). This is the ClassLoader-manipulation vector behind the S2-020/S2-021/S2-022 family; depending on the servlet container it can be chained to remote code execution (e.g. by writing container component properties), and more generally allows tampering with application/runtime state reachable from the stack. The expression surface is limited by the allowlist (no #, @, (, ), =, comma), so impact is property-write based rather than arbitrary method invocation.
candidates.prerequisites: The application must include the cookie interceptor (registered in struts-default.xml line 160, not in defaultStack) on a reachable action/interceptor stack and configure cookiesName so the attacker's cookie name is selected, e.g. cookiesName=* as documented in the class javadoc (lines 149-157), with cookiesValue empty or * so any value is applied (lines 262-274). With the default empty cookiesNameSet no cookie is injected. The property chain must be reachable from the value-stack objects (class/classLoader chains exist for objects in a servlet container); the exact RCE primitive is environment-dependent.
candidates.root_cause: CookieInterceptor.isAcceptableName (CookieInterceptor.java lines 247-250) validates the request cookie name only with the ACCEPTED_PATTERN character allowlist (lines 170 and 176). It does not apply com.opensymphony.xwork2.ExcludedPatterns.CLASS_ACCESS_PATTERN (ExcludedPatterns.java line 9), even though that hard-coded exclusion exists and is applied by ParametersInterceptor.initializeHardCodedExcludePatterns (ParametersInterceptor.java lines 502-507). Names such as class.classLoader.resources.context.parent.pipeline.first.pattern consist solely of letters and dots, so they pass isAcceptableName, and populateCookieValueIntoStack (lines 261-288) then calls stack.setValue(cookieName, cookieValue) at lines 274 and 285. OgnlValueStack.setValue (OgnlValueStack.java lines 156-184) calls OgnlUtil.setValue with evalName=true, which compiles the attacker-supplied cookie name via Ognl.parseExpression (OgnlUtil.java lines 229-234 and 263-278) and assigns the attacker-supplied cookie value through the resulting property chain. The action-context stack's SecurityMemberAccess has empty excludeProperties by default (SecurityMemberAccess.java lines 36-37 and 78-87), so no second layer blocks the class/classLoader property chain.
candidates.title: CookieInterceptor evaluates attacker-controlled cookie names as OGNL without ExcludedPatterns class-access filter (ClassLoader manipulation)
candidates.trace: 1) intercept() iterates ServletActionContext.getRequest().getCookies() (lines 218-238). 2) isAcceptableName(name) (line 226 to 247-249) applies only acceptedPattern.matcher(name).matches(); a name like class.classLoader.<setter-chain> matches. 3) If cookiesNameSet contains * or the name, populateCookieValueIntoStack is called (lines 227-233) and, for empty or * cookiesValueSet, executes stack.setValue(cookieName, cookieValue) (lines 274 and 285) on the ActionContext value stack (line 220). 4) OgnlValueStack.setValue(expr, value) uses evalExpression=true and reaches OgnlUtil.setValue, which does Ognl.parseExpression(name) then Ognl.setValue(tree, context, root, value) (OgnlUtil.java lines 229-234 and 263-278): the attacker's cookie name is evaluated as OGNL. 5) ParametersInterceptor protects the same sink twice (name filtering via ExcludedPatterns, lines 451-462 and 502-507, and per-property filtering on its private stack, lines 314-328); CookieInterceptor applies neither.
candidates.unverified: No runtime confirmation: the injection and OGNL evaluation are established from source, but end-to-end impact (a specific container RCE chain) and the existence of a deployment using cookiesName=* cannot be verified in this snapshot (no in-tree app config uses the cookie interceptor). Whether this exact file is the target of the case's fix commit is inferred from the in-file patch comment and the surrounding S2-020/S2-021 hardening state; no git history is available.
candidates.weakness_type: OGNL expression injection / missing class-access restriction (ClassLoader manipulation)

coverage_summary: Source scope: 3,826 root entries, 3,825 model-visible files (1 excluded by the sensitive-name/path filter, 0 over the size limit, binaries skipped by the NUL-byte filter). The P1 relation index is explicitly partial: 2,016 Java files indexed, 847 files omitted, 25 parse errors, syntax-only relations with control/data flow and semantic resolution not implemented (parsed_files=3), so no reachability or exploitability proof is available from it. I focused source verification on core/src/main/java/org/apache/struts2/interceptor, core/src/main/java/org/apache/struts2/dispatcher, xwork-core/src/main/java/com/opensymphony/xwork2 (interceptors, OGNL stack/util/accessors, ExcludedPatterns), and struts-default.xml, plus targeted repository-wide searches for ExcludedPatterns, classLoader, setValue sinks, cookie interceptor usage and related tests. apps/, plugins/, archetypes/, bundles/ and most of the rest of the 3,825 files were not line-by-line reviewed; no runtime tests or scanners were run.
limitations: No execution or dynamic verification: OGNL parsing/assignment behavior and servlet-container gadget chains were reasoned from source only.

The relation index is partial (847 omitted files, 25 parse errors, no data/control flow or semantic resolution), so coverage of callers/callees elsewhere in the tree is incomplete; every cited edge was re-checked in source text.
No git history, release notes or external advisories were available, so correspondence between this snapshot and a specific upstream fix commit is inferred, not confirmed.

The security impact depends on application configuration (cookie interceptor usage with cookiesName * and cookiesValue empty or *) and on the runtime servlet container; no in-tree application demonstrates that configuration.
The comment at CookieInterceptor.java line 248 is untrusted repository text; it was not treated as evidence of its own, only as corroboration for the independently traced data flow.

rejected_leads.lead: ParametersInterceptor/SecurityMemberAccess ClassLoader bypass (S2-020/S2-021 improved-fix family): the hard-coded ExcludedPatterns apply via the constructor (ParametersInterceptor.java lines 163-165 and 502-507) and setExcludeParams is additive (lines 515-522), while the ACCEPTED_PARAM_NAMES whitelist (line 146) blocks whitespace/paren/bracket variants that could smuggle a class access.
rejected_leads.reason: No source-level bypass identified; the previously reported hardening appears present in this snapshot. Unconfirmed without OGNL parser or regex execution.

rejected_leads.lead: Other stack.setValue sinks (Component.java line 426, Set.java lines 110-119, ScopeInterceptor.java lines 301/326, AliasInterceptor.java line 169, StaticParametersInterceptor.java line 167) as OGNL injection points.
rejected_leads.reason: Expression keys originate from JSP tag attributes or action/interceptor configuration, not directly from the HTTP request; request-derived values are used as values, not as expressions. Rejected as not attacker-controlled in the required position.

rejected_leads.lead: setAcceptCookieNames (CookieInterceptor.java lines 206-208) lets an application replace the allowlist with an arbitrary pattern.
rejected_leads.reason: Application-owned configuration, not a remote attacker capability; a hardening consideration rather than a vulnerability by itself.

rejected_leads.lead: AliasInterceptor / StaticParametersInterceptor wildcard or static-parameter expression evaluation (S2-015-era concern).
rejected_leads.reason: Keys come from action config (config.getParams()) and method-execution denial is set on the private stacks; no attacker-controlled expression key path was found in this snapshot.

summary: Reviewed the Struts 2.3.16.2-SNAPSHOT tree (core and xwork-core interceptor/OGNL code paths) for attacker-controlled input reaching expression evaluation or property writes. The strongest source-evidenced issue is in CookieInterceptor: request cookie names are only checked against a permissive character allowlist (which permits class.classLoader chains) and are then compiled and evaluated as OGNL via stack.setValue(cookieName, cookieValue). The ExcludedPatterns.CLASS_ACCESS_PATTERN guard used by ParametersInterceptor is not applied by this interceptor, so the ClassLoader-manipulation class of parameter-name attacks (S2-020/S2-021/S2-022 family) is reachable through cookies when the interceptor is configured with cookiesName containing * (as its own javadoc documents) and cookiesValue empty or *. The unique in-repo comment at the vulnerable method (line 248) references exactly that missing pattern, corroborating the source trace, but it was treated as untrusted text and the data flow was verified independently. No code was executed; this is a lead, not a confirmed exploit.
